Mount Cotopaxi. An active stratovolcano located in the Andes Mountains of Ecuador, Cotopaxi is one of the highest active volcanoes in the world, rising to an elevation of nineteen thousand three hundred forty-seven feet. It features a nearly symmetrical, snow-capped cone and is home to one of the world's few equatorial glaciers. The glacier is highly prone to melting during eruptions and causes devastating mudflows. Cotopaxi threatens the nearby city of Latacunga, which has been buried and rebuilt multiple times throughout history due to massive volcanic mudflows called lahars racing down the mountain's valleys. The volcano was first climbed successfully in 1872 by German geologist Wilhelm Reiss and Colombian explorer Angel Escobar. It was also depicted in a famous 1862 landscape painting by Frederic Edwin Church, a prominent member of the American Hudson River School of artists. Mount Cotopaxi stands as a peer active stratovolcano to Vesuvius, known for its classic symmetrical shape, and resembles Mount Erebus, another high-altitude active volcano famous for its glacial ice features.
